text: A VPC or VNet on its own is just one big address range, so in practice you break it into smaller subnets — the same subnetting math from Chapter 1, just applied inside the cloud instead of on physical hardware. A common pattern splits one VPC into a public subnet for a load balancer or bastion host, and separate private subnets for application servers and the database layer behind them.

A route table is a set of rules deciding where traffic leaving a subnet gets sent next, and every subnet is associated with one. The rule that matters most is whether that table has a route to an internet gateway. A public subnet's route table sends unmatched traffic out to the internet gateway. A private subnet has no such route at all, so nothing inside it can reach the internet directly, no matter how its security rules are configured.

A security group is a firewall attached directly to a resource, like an EC2 instance, not to the subnet it sits in. It's stateful, meaning if you allow inbound traffic on a connection, the matching outbound reply is automatically allowed back out without a separate rule. A network ACL, by contrast, attaches to the subnet itself and is stateless: inbound and outbound rules are evaluated completely independently, and unlike a security group, it can explicitly deny traffic rather than only allow it.

Azure's equivalent of a security group is the Network Security Group, or NSG — same stateful, attached-to-the-resource model, just a different vendor's name for essentially the same idea. Whichever cloud you're in, the pattern is the same: a resource-level firewall for everyday rules, and a subnet-level firewall for broader, explicit allow-or-deny control.

Next lesson: load balancing fundamentals — how traffic gets spread across more than one backend server instead of hitting a single point of failure, and the real difference between routing by IP and port versus routing by the actual content of a request.
